sections.title: Artist's Statement
paragraphs: As Augusto Boal proposed, theater is the rehearsal for the revolution. If the stage is a space to imagine and practice the world we want, then the question becomes: when the lights go out, how do we integrate what we have rehearsed?

That question drives my practice. In a moment when atrocities continue to unfold around the world and our communities are increasingly divided against one another, theater can remind us that the systems oppressing us are not the same things as the people standing besides us.
At the center of my practice are five main principals:

Resourcefulness - in an effort to model a zero waste theater, production elements – from props and costumes to technical equipment – are salvaged, borrowed, donated, found, or made from other people’s trash. This is both an environmental practice and a political one. It challenges the assumption that meaningful art requires endless resources and asks what becomes possible when we treat what we already have as valuable.

Community Care - My hierarchy is simple : people over process and process over product. I believe that excellence emerges when artists are cared for, trusted, and given the space to be fully human. In doing so, we cultivate something increasingly precious: an artistic offering grounded in human connection, collaboration, and care – qualities that cannot be replicated by AI.

Honoring the past – Each project is an opportunity to honor those who made my own existence and artistic practice possible. I look to the histories of queer people, immigrants, and other communities who have had to invent new ways of living in a world that criminalizes them. Their survival is evidence of our capacity to imagine otherwise.

Creative agency – My model of theatermaking is built on self generated incentive, collective ownership, and creative agency. The result has been projects in which artists invest more time, energy, and love because they have genuine ownership of what they are creating, elevating the work precisely because it is communally owned. I see this not only as a model for making theater, but as a model for imagining institutions, workplaces, and society itself.
Play - is essential to that imagining. What better way to return us to ourselves and remind us what we are fighting for than through play?

In these ways, art can function simultaneously as social work, therapy, community building, education, cultural preservation, and political organizing. It can provide sanctuary and release from the grueling conditions of American life while also giving us the tools to transform those conditions. It gives us the rare opportunity to gather in the same room, imagine together, laugh together, grieve together, and remind us of our humanity. At a time when we are increasingly under threat, that gathering is not a luxury - it is a rehearsal for another world.
